text: Chapter fourteen, design YouTube. In three minutes, see how a video is split into chunks, processed in parallel, and put back together.

Start with the big picture. When a client uploads a video, the API only handles authentication and metadata. It never touches the video bytes. The video goes straight into object storage. Transcoding servers turn it into several versions, and a CDN delivers them to viewers. Upload once, convert into many, play from the edge.

The original file can be hundreds of megabytes, so one big upload fails easily. Instead, we split it into small chunks and upload them in parallel. The API authenticates the user and issues a time-limited pre-signed URL. With it, the client sends every chunk directly to object storage. If one chunk fails, only that chunk is retried. This is resumable upload.

Transcoding also works on chunks, but we can't cut at random bytes. Video frames depend on each other: later frames refer back to an earlier key frame. So the preprocessor cuts at GOP boundaries, short for group of pictures. Every chunk starts with a key frame, so it can be decoded and processed on its own.

Next, the preprocessor builds a directed acyclic graph from the configuration. The original is first split into video, audio, and metadata. The video then fans out into encodings at several resolutions and bitrates, plus thumbnails and a watermark. Tasks with no dependencies between them can run at the same time.

The scheduler puts tasks into the resource manager's queue, then picks idle workers to run them. Here, eight chunks are shared among three workers. If a task fails, only that chunk is retried, and intermediate results sit in temporary storage. When everything is done, the pieces are merged into the final output.

One more trap: when is transcoding really finished? If the completion event arrives before the file is on disk, the user sees a playable video, clicks it, and gets a four-oh-four. So wait until the output and the manifest are persisted and verified, and only then publish the ready status. Higher resolutions can become available later.

For playback, the client first fetches a manifest, then downloads the video segment by segment. Protocols include MPEG-DASH and Apple HLS. Adaptive bitrate switches between quality levels based on network throughput and buffer. When the network slows down, drop one level. The goal is no stalling.

These segments come from the CDN edge node closest to the viewer. On a hit, it returns immediately. On a miss, the edge goes back to the origin, fetches the segment, and caches it, so the next viewer gets a hit. Popular videos are served almost entirely from the edge.

The key trade-off is cost. Under the book's assumptions, five million daily active users each watch five videos of three hundred megabytes. That makes the CDN bill one hundred fifty thousand dollars a day. But viewing has a long tail. Popular videos go through the CDN. Unpopular ones come from high-capacity servers, or are even transcoded on demand. The price is slower first play and more load on the origin.
Remember three phrases: chunked upload, DAG-based parallel transcoding, and CDN playback. Cost depends on viewing traffic and cache hits, not just the unit price.
